subtype: Approach: starts long-lead items early and does small tasks in the gaps [Action]
passage:
Subject: Where we are with the wedding plan

Dear Ujjwal,

A quick update on the first week. Before anything else, I placed the order for the printed invitation cards on Monday. The printer needs two weeks, and every other date, such as sending them out and counting guests, depends on them. While they are being printed, I have used the waiting time for shorter jobs: three calls to caterers, a hall visit on Wednesday and a confirmation with the decorator. None of these needed the cards, and none will take more than a day. If the cards arrive on the fourteenth as promised, we can send them on the fifteenth. I will email you the caterers' quotes tomorrow.

Regards,
Gurpreet

qa.q: How long does the printer need for the cards?
qa.a: The printer needs two weeks.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet want from ordering the cards first?
qa.a: Gurpreet wants the slowest job started early so that it does not hold up every other date.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet do if the printer is late?
qa.a: Gurpreet could ask the printer for a firm date, prepare a digital invitation to send meanwhile, and tell Ujjwal early.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel on reading the update?
qa.a: Ujjwal may feel reassured that the slowest job is under way and that progress is visible.

grounding: Shows a planner ordering the slowest item first and filling the waiting time with shorter jobs such as calls.

subtype: Approach: focuses on the visible tasks and ignores a hidden dependency [Pitfall]
passage:
Day 1. In the app team's room, Parveen admired the new checkout screens: fresh colours, smoother buttons. "Launch on the first of next month," Parveen said. The team spent the following days tuning animations and fonts.

Day 20. Bhavna looked up from a laptop. "Has anyone applied for the payment approval?" Silence. Nobody had listed it. Parveen opened the provider's page and read aloud, "It takes about a month."

Day 30. The first of the month came and went, with a beautiful app that could not take a single payment. The launch moved by four weeks, and the client had to be told.

qa.q: How long does the payment approval take?
qa.a: The approval takes about a month.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt on opening the provider's page?
qa.a: Parveen probably felt shocked and worried, since the approval was on no list and the date could not be met.

qa.q: What could the team have done at the start?
qa.a: The team could have listed every step to launch, including outside approvals, and started the slowest one first.

qa.q: How might the client feel on being told the launch moved?
qa.a: The client might feel disappointed or concerned, having expected the first of the month.

grounding: Shows a team polishing visible screens while an unlisted approval that takes a month delays the launch.

subtype: Approach: redraws the path when a delay appears and shifts resources [Revision]
passage:
Sabina: Your launch slipped once. How did you handle it?

Gopika: The security review we needed came back two weeks late. My first feeling was panic, honestly. Then I redrew the board and asked which tasks now decided the end date. Testing the checkout and the data move, because they waited on the review's answer. So I shifted two developers off the animations and the settings page and onto those two. Everything that could wait, waited: the dark theme, the help page, the extra language. People grumbled about the dark theme. I said it would go in the next release. We launched five days after the new date instead of two weeks.

Sabina: What would you do differently?

Gopika: Draw that board on day one.

qa.q: Which two tasks did the two developers move onto?
qa.a: The two developers moved onto testing the checkout and the data move.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel at first when the review came back late?
qa.a: Gopika felt panic, honestly, at the start.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Gopika's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Gopika redrew the board to see which tasks now decided the end date, then moved people to them, so the delay shrank.

qa.q: How might the people who wanted the dark theme have felt?
qa.a: They grumbled, and may have felt their work was being set aside, until they heard it would go in the next release.

grounding: Shows a lead redrawing the path after a delay and moving developers to the tasks that now determine the end date.

passage: I am Tanuja, and painting is my favourite thing. Before, I washed my brush after every colour and put each tube away straight after using it. It took so long that I ran out of time to paint. subtype: Approach: groups similar homework into one session [Action]
passage:
Dear Himani,

Guess what changed my evenings? Last week I bounced from history reading to maths to history writing to English reading, and after two hours I had barely done a thing. My pencil kept going missing and I kept losing my place. So on Monday I tried something different: first all the reading tasks in a row (the history chapter, the English poem, my science notes), thirty-five minutes. Then a short break. Then all the writing: history answers, an English paragraph, the lab record. It took one hour forty minutes and I finished before dinner. Switching costs me more than I thought. Try it and tell me if it works for you too.

Tushar

qa.q: How long did the reading block last?
qa.a: The reading block took thirty-five minutes.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel about the old way of working?
qa.a: Tushar felt frustrated, having done little in two hours and lost the place again and again.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the writing block feels too long?
qa.a: Tushar could split it into two short parts with a stretch between, keeping similar tasks together.

qa.q: How might Himani see Tushar's tip?
qa.a: Himani might be curious and glad to test whether it works for Himani's own study.

grounding: Shows a student grouping all reading tasks and then all writing tasks into separate sessions to avoid switching.

subtype: Approach: batches errands into one trip [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Nirmala,

Quick note on how I stopped wasting Saturdays. In my first month I went to town three times in one week: once for a notebook, once for the laundry pick-up, once for the bank. Each trip was a bus ride and forty minutes of waiting. Last week I stopped and thought: these three are all in the same market. Why go three times? So I wrote a list on the back of my hand: stationery, laundry, bank. I went to the bank first, before it got crowded, then the stationery shop, then the laundry on the way back to the bus. One trip, done by twelve. I even had time to sit with a cold drink. The free hours felt like a present.

Noor

qa.q: What three errands were on Noor's list?
qa.a: Noor's list said stationery, laundry, bank.

qa.q: How did Noor feel about the extra free hours?
qa.a: Noor felt pleased, saying that the free hours felt like a present.

qa.q: What could Noor check before the next trip?
qa.a: Noor could check that the shops are open that day and that all three are near the bus stop, so the trip works.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel on reading this news?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel relieved and proud that Noor is managing time and cutting extra trips.

grounding: Shows a hostel student combining stationery, laundry and a bank visit into one trip instead of three.

subtype: Approach: batches emails in fixed slots to protect deep work [Action]
passage: I'm Jagdish, and for two years my mornings belonged to the chat window. Every ping pulled me out of my code, and by lunch I had written very little. Last spring I changed one rule: I read messages at eleven and at four, and at no other time. I told the team. Indu, who leads our group, asked, "And if it's urgent?" I said, "Call me." I muted the chat and closed the tab. The first days were itchy; I kept wanting to check. But by the second week I was finishing the hard parts of a feature before eleven, and at eleven I answered everything at once without losing my thread. So far nobody has needed to call.

qa.q: At what times does Jagdish read messages?
qa.a: Jagdish reads messages at eleven and at four.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel in the first days of the new rule?
qa.a: Jagdish felt itchy, wanting to check the chat all the time.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do so that urgent matters still get through?
qa.a: Jagdish could make sure the team knows which matters count as urgent and how to call, as agreed with Indu.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about the change?
qa.a: Indu might feel worried at first about urgent matters, and reassured by "Call me" as a clear route.

grounding: Shows a developer reading messages only at fixed times so the morning stays free for coding.

subtype: Approach: batches so long that urgent matters wait too long [Pitfall]
passage: Lars had read that answering messages once a day saves time, so from Monday he opened the team chat only at five o'clock. On Wednesday at ten past nine in the Rotterdam office, Tuan wrote: "The client asks whether the delivery can move to Thursday. They need an answer before noon." Tuan waited, wrote again at eleven, and again at half past twelve. Lars was in meetings and did not look. By noon Tuan had told the client, "I'll get back to you today." The client, who had another supplier ready, went with them. At five Lars read all the messages together and went cold. "Why didn't you call me?" Tuan said, "You said no calls unless it's an emergency, and I didn't know if this counted."

qa.q: At what time did Lars open the team chat?
qa.a: Lars opened the team chat only at five o'clock.

qa.q: How did Lars feel on reading the messages at five?
qa.a: Lars felt shocked and regretful, and went cold.

qa.q: What could Lars do so that urgent questions are seen?
qa.a: Lars could keep the fixed message slots but agree on a call or a flagged word for urgent client matters, and check for it more often.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt while waiting through the morning?
qa.a: Tuan may have felt anxious and stuck, unsure whether to phone, as the client's deadline came closer.

grounding: Shows a manager answering messages only once a day so a colleague's urgent client question sits unanswered until evening.
